note: Authored pronunciation help, one entry per phoneme declared in data/phonology/phonology.json. Keys are phoneme ids; tests/learningContent.test.ts fails if a declared phoneme has no entry or an entry names a phoneme that does not exist, so this file cannot drift from the inventory. `en` and `nl` are anchor words a learner already knows how to say; `how` is the instruction for a sound neither language has.

p.how: Unaspirated: no puff of air after it, closer to the Dutch p than the English one.

t.how: Unaspirated, tongue against the ridge behind the teeth.

k.how: Unaspirated. Note that k and kh are different sounds, not a spelling variation.

g.nl: g in goal (the loanword g, not the Dutch native g)
g.how: A hard g. Dutch speakers: this is NOT the Dutch g in 'goed' — that sound is gh.

q.how: A k made much further back, with the very back of the tongue against the soft palate — a deep, swallowed k. Say 'kar', then make the same sound as far back in the throat as you can.

gh.how: A voiced scrape at the back of the mouth. Dutch and Flemish speakers already have this; English speakers can start from a gargle and soften it.

kh.how: The voiceless partner of gh: same place, no voice.

zh.how: The voiced partner of sh. Never starts a word.

ng.how: One sound, not n followed by g. Never starts a word.

r.nl: r in rood (Gooise or throat r)
r.how: Trilled at the back of the throat, like French or standard German r. This is the sound that gives the language its growl — do not substitute an English r.

l.how: Always a clear l, never the dark l English uses at the end of 'full'.

w.nl: w in wauw (not the Dutch w in 'water')
w.how: Dutch speakers: lips rounded, no teeth — the English w.

th.how: Tongue tip between the teeth, no voice. Dutch speakers: this is not s and not t — let the air hiss over the tongue tip.

â.how: The long partner of a. Length is meaningful: hold it.

ê.en: e in they, without the glide

ô.en: o in more, without the r
